newsitem.title: UK: BA flies the flag for privatisation.
newsitem.headline: BA flies the flag for privatisation.

text.p: British Airways Plc was flying high celebrating 10 years in the private sector on Monday, reporting record profits and offering supersonic round trips to New York on Concorde for 10 pounds ($16.30).

The self-styled "World's Favourite Airline" is no stranger to criticism, humiliated in court four years ago by rival Virgin Atlantic over allegations of dirty tricks and now under fire over a proposed alliance with American Airlines.

But even if the anniversary of its share selloff on Tuesday attracts as many brickbats as bouquets from rivals, it has proved a paragon of privatisation for Britain's Conservative government and other countries seeking to sell off their own national flag carriers.
Earlier the carrier announced profits for the nine months to December 31 at an all-time high of 583 million pounds pre-tax, up from the previous record of 534 million for the same period a year ago.
It also launched a special anniversary promotion offering 10 seats on every return flight by Concorde from London to New York during the 10 days from February 12.
To get the seats people have to telephone the main BA sales office at 2200 GMT on Tuesday.

Now ranked as one the world's most profitable airlines and the biggest international carrier, BA says it has made 3.24 billion pounds in taxable profits in the last decade, paid over 600 million pounds in tax and 800 million pounds in dividends.
"I think they have done very well," said Nigel Hawkins, European utilities and transport analyst for Yamaichi International.

"There is absolutely no doubt at all that BA's privatisation has raised customer standards very considerably indeed...and they have had to earn their revenues through customers as opposed to regulators," he said.

"If you compare BA with British Gas, who were privatised at roughly the same time, one has done terribly well in competitive markets and made itself a global name. The other is now locked in a pitched battle with its regulator."

Many other privatised utilities have been keeping a low profile since Britain's opposition Labour Party vowed to target "windfall" tax targets if it wins the next election, accusing the Conservatives of selling them off too cheaply.
But BA is confident enough to raise its head above the parapet to boast of its success for shareholders and the British economy alike.
"Our understanding from what we have heard Labour politicians say is that the windfall tax is aimed at monopoly utilities," said a company spokesman.
"BA is not a utility, neither is it a monopoly. We compete with around 100 airlines in the UK alone," he said.

Critics say BA couldn't fail to succeed since it holds 38 percent of all runway capacity at London Heathrow, the world's biggest international airport -- the issue at the centre of controversy surrounding BA's alliance with American.
But this was of little advantage to the airline when it was a loss-making state carrier dubbed "BA for Bloody Awful" by many travellers.

Shareholders who bought in the flotation at 125 pence a share on February 11, 1987 would have received a total of 100.7 pence in dividends and seen the share price rise to the 598-1/2 prevailing on Monday, the airline said.
BA says it has also created more than 16,000 jobs since 1987, with the workforce growing from 40,759 staff at privatisation to 57,644 currently, including acquisitions and staff cutbacks.

The size of its fleet has nearly doubled from 164 aircraft in 1987 to 295 now and in that time it has carried 285 million passngers on almost three million flights, equivalent to a take-off or landing every minute of the day. ($1=.6120 Pound)
